content_metadata.description: This video critically examines and debunks the Noah's Ark flood myth using geological evidence and experiments.

qAndA.answer: He misinterprets volcanic ash deposits and pyroclastic flow as a mudflow.

qAndA.answer: The video states that chalk can build up at a rate of up to 2 inches per thousand years.

qAndA.answer: The narrator adds different types of sediment (stones, sand, silt, etc.) to a container of water and stirs it. He then observes that the sediment settles into a single layer, not distinct layers as Hovind claims.
qAndA.question: What experiment does the narrator perform to challenge Hovind's claim about sediment layering?

qAndA.answer: The narrator uses chalk cliffs as an example of slow deposition, explaining their formation from coccolithophores over millions of years.
qAndA.question: What type of geological formation does the narrator present as evidence for the slow, gradual deposition of sediment?

qAndA.answer: The overall mood is critical and skeptical, with the narrator challenging creationist claims and encouraging viewers to think critically about the evidence.

Grand Canyon. 200 years ago the first geologists believed absolutely what the Bible told them,
and set forth to find traces of this great flood. Their view of the world was pretty much
the same as creationist today. God had made the earth mostly out of granite and basalt,
then along came the flood bearing and preserving all the animals and plants under a massive
muddy sediment. Then life returned, the soil was built up, and today we live on top of
all these remains. And if you listen to creationists on this subject, this is exactly what geologists
have found. But when early geologists looked at these water-lane rocks more closely, they
got a surprise, because they didn't find this at all. They found something more like this.
They found layers of different types of rock, in no particular order. No sign of that single
global flood deposit anywhere. Kent Hoveon pretends not to be surprised. He says we should get

add some water to it, shake it up, and set it now. It settles into layers for you. This is an

to find out what happens. Let's do it for him. To test the Hoveon Theory, add different flood

soil, natural topsoil from the forest, and a bit of vegetation, add water and stir. Let's leave
it to settle for a bit and look at more of the Hoveon Theory. When you put out into the canyons
near Mousain Hallons, you will see erosion. It was incredible there, and it has the sides of the
canyon are stratified, nice neat layers. They said, oh wait a minute, all this mud flowed in here
at one time. Why is it stratified? Did Hoveon just say this was mud? Wait a minute, all this mud flowed

Knowing that Hoveon is predisposed to lying through his teeth, I tracked down the picture to a

The caption on the photo confirms it, it says the bottom layer formed on May 18, 1980,
and the middle one a month later. So not only are these two separate layers, both dates go inside
with eruptions of pyroclasts from Mousain Hallons, not mud flows. Pyroclasts is basically particulate
matter rejected from a volcano as distinct from gas and lava. Only the top layer is identified
in the caption as a mud flow, and one that occurred two years later. So not only did they not
form at one time as Hoveon claims, they're not even flood deposits. Why is this important? Or to
put it another way, why is it important enough for Hoveon to want to lie about it? Well, creationists
are using Mousain Hallons to argue that a single sedimentary event can form distinctive layers,
and therefore a global flood could have done the same. But as we've seen, Mousain Hallons was a
series of separate events, most of which were volcanic and not flood-related. A single flood
doesn't produce separate layers of different material, it produces a single layer, a graded
material. I'll let Hoveon prove my point by going back to the experiment, he obviously never

Corsa grains and heavy gravels tend to be found at the bottom, and smaller and lighter material
like silts and muds are generally found nearer the top. It may look as though there are two or
three separate layers here, but on closer inspection you can see the different grain sizes and the

clearly defined sedimentary layers, each made of different material, and in no particular order.
This photo shows a layer of red limestone topped by chalk. So if Hoveon's flood experiments spectacularly
fails to recreate these separate layers, what would do it? Well let's add the same materials again,
this time recreating the kind of conditions we see on earth today. First, sprinkle some mud to

today being deposited in some deltas, and finally a layer of larger stones to represent a conglomerate.
And presto, we've recreated the layering we see in the rocks all around us. None of this is magic,
I'm just recreating the kind of deposition we see in different environments all over the world today.
And it fits perfectly with the distinct layering of separate materials we see in the rocks all around us.

textbooks for the last 150 years. We know that some sedimentary material like pyroclast,
flood deposit, and breccia is deposited very rapidly. But to argue that all sediments that
therefore deposited quickly is nonsense. In fact, we know they aren't.
Take chalk, for example. It's made of the shells of trillions of marine algae called
coccolithophores. As these organisms die, their shell plates, called coccoliths, fall to the bottom
of the sea and accumulate, building up a layer of chalk at a rate of up to two inches every thousand

What you're hearing is the sound of creationists rushing to answers in Genesis.com to find out

But even if that was chemically possible and didn't break all the laws of thermodynamics,

Fossilized coral represents another problem for the flood story. It's obviously not a flood

intelligent examination of the rocks shows a very different story. These rocks present no great
mystery for geologists because they made of exactly the same sediment being laid down in different
environments today, from the slow deposition of chalk and limestone to the rapid deposition
caused by local floods and mudslides to the steady buildup of sandstones and siltstones.
If creationists like Hovein prefer to sit in their armchairs and make up what they call theories,
then there's a very easy way for them to support their case.

will miraculously separate into different layers.
No it's no good going to answers in Genesis.com. They've never done the experiment.
The last thing you want to do when you've got a theory that's wrong is do an experiment that'll
prove it wrong. But we live in the 21st century where we don't have to just accept these
Bronze Age stories because Sunday school teachers tell us they're true. We're capable of thinking
